summary:
Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain with no LGTBI or gender-identity statute of its own. It stands under the national framework of Ley 4/2023 and central-government policy, and no regional ordinance supplements them, so a trans visitor deals directly with Spanish law and Spanish institutions rather than with any local statute.

FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ public policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, names Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. The report records legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla.

The gap is not new. A 2020 precedent study cited in the same body of work placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of rankings for the recognition and protection of trans students.

Protection questions in Ceuta also run through migration. Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli described transfer as the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people fleeing criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta.

For a visitor, the practical consequence is that no regional layer of LGTBI+ policy exists to consult or appeal to: recognition, anti-discrimination and criminal-law protection operate through the national framework, and the documented deficit is one of regional legislation and regional-level provision rather than of a hostile local statute.
tangentialFactors:
Ceuta's position in national rankings reflects the absence of a regional law, not the presence of a restrictive one. The city applies the same national equality and criminal-law framework as the rest of Spain; what it lacks is the additional regional statute and regional policy machinery that most autonomous communities have adopted.

The city's geography as a North African enclave on the Strait of Gibraltar places a population of LGTBI+ migrants inside its boundaries whose protection depends on transfer to the mainland. That situation is specific to Ceuta and Melilla among Spanish territories and is separate from the question of visitor-facing law.
localsOnly:
Residents of Ceuta have no regional LGTBI+ or trans-specific statute to invoke and rely on the national framework together with central-government policies. The FELGTBI+ and Universidad de Salamanca review of September 2025 lists the city among four territories without a specific law on promotion of LGTBI+ rights, alongside Asturias, Castilla y León and Melilla, and records no legislative step for Ceuta during 2025.

Trans students in Ceuta were placed at the bottom of a 2020 ranking of recognition and protection, alongside Melilla. LGTBI+ migrants held in the city after the entries of 30 and 31 July 2026 have access to a free remote social, psychological and legal support service set up by Arcópoli, which has argued that only transfer to the peninsula secures their protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no region-specific record of enforcement action, hate incidents, facility access, healthcare provision or police practice in Ceuta. Whether the city operates any municipal protocol, service or equality body is not sourced.

The 2020 study placing Ceuta at the tail of trans-student rankings is cited second-hand through the 2025 review; its methodology, indicators and sample are not described in the available material, so the ranking cannot be assessed beyond its stated position.

The number of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after the July 2026 entries, and the outcome of Arcópoli's request to the Secretary of State for Migration, are not established in the sources.
